proposed_edges.relationship: In “Alfred G. Bailey — Ethnohistorian” (1989), Trigger criticizes Innis for explaining Indigenous participation in the fur trade through universal economic rationality while neglecting particular beliefs and ways of life.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the official Acadiensis PDF, printed p. 5, first paragraph and nn. 7–8 (PDF leaf 3): Innis’s participants become “‘Economic Man’ dressed up in feathers.” Trigger nevertheless credits Innis with recognizing their important role in obtaining furs; n. 8 preserves his acknowledgment of their cultural importance. The note refers back to Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985), pp. 183–184, which were not read. The proposal rests on the 1989 passage, not those unread pages or a claim that Innis simply ignored Indigenous people.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: explain their participation in terms of universal patterns of rational economic behaviour... 'Economic Man' dressed up in feathers
review.reason: Official Acadiensis PDF, printed p. 5: Innis 'paid little attention to how their specific beliefs and ways of life influenced their participation'. Sentence is accurate and keeps Trigger's acknowledgement of Innis. n. 8 points to Natives and Newcomers pp. 183-4 (unread, correctly excluded).

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger contests Kuhnian incommensurability and revolutionary replacement as explanations of archaeological theory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 8–9: rival positions are “not incommensurate”; gradual change and recurring positions challenge replacement. He acknowledges Kuhn’s qualifications (pp. 6–7). This reading concerns the 2006 revision; the 1989 first edition is unread.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: Thus, they are not incommensurate with one another in the Kuhnian sense... I will avoid the term 'paradigm'
review.reason: Publisher excerpt pp. 8-9: rival archaeological positions coexist, 'no evidence that they are trapped in noncommunicating discourses'; Kuhn 'failed to account for the longevity of various positions'. Some objections are reported from Chapman, Schiffer, VanPool, but Trigger adopts them in his own voice. Front matter confirms 1989 first / 2006 second edition; claim correctly bounded to 2006.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger criticizes Foucault’s epistemes for underestimating overlap and inadequately explaining archaeology’s simultaneous theoretical diversity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 9–10: “Epistemes can contribute little” to explaining concurrent diversity. He allows potential value. Only this introductory passage was checked; no first-edition attribution is made.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: Foucault also appears to underestimate the extent to which epistemes have overlapped... Epistemes can contribute little
review.reason: Excerpt pp. 9-10 matches; Trigger allows 'potentially valuable contributions'. Bounded to the 2006 edition.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing the French translation (1990) of Trigger's Natives and Newcomers (1985) in 1992, Dickason endorses as 'un argument de taille' his warning that excessive reliance on written records distorts Indigenous history, while stressing that archaeological evidence also poses problems of interpretation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading: Persée HTML p. 284 identifies the translation and original 1985 publication; p. 285, second paragraph, reads “L’auteur invoque un argument de taille” after summarizing Trigger’s warning. The following sentences stress incomplete records and interpretation problems. Page 285 was read in the project’s previously saved official Persée HTML and visually checked against its saved official image. The Sioui discussion begins in the next paragraph and is excluded. Neither version of Trigger’s book was read; this is a bounded review response, not a personal debt. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Persée p. 285 text read directly (not only a saved copy); p. 284 gives 1985 original date. Content of the sentence is supported. Direction/kind is the problem: Dickason did not contribute to Trigger; she received and endorsed his argument. Project precedent for 'X recommends/endorses Y's work' is Y -> X contribution (e.g. edge_2965 james_rodger_miller -> emma_larocque; jrm_bf_02 in this packet). Reverse the direction; sentence can stand.]

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger invokes Carr’s argument that selecting relevant evidence presupposes theory against a model of archaeological data collection preceding explanation.
proposed_edges.map_label: Carr on theory in selecting evidence
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, p. 5: explicitly credits Carr (1967: 3–35). A named methodological resource, not mentorship. Carr’s cited edition and Trigger’s first edition were not read.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: E. H. Carr (1967: 3–35) has reminded us... characterization of data as being relevant or irrelevant... implies... theoretical framework
review.reason: Excerpt p. 5 matches, set against Willey and Sabloff's inductive Baconian collect-then-explain model. Named methodological resource, bounded to 2006 edition. Carr 1967 is a reprint of What Is History? (1961); the edge does not date Carr's work, so no correction needed.
